Pitch, loudness, duration, timbre, sonic texture, and spatial location are perceptions with physical correlates, not measurements: the ear hears a missing fundamental, fills short gaps, and finds tones near 3 kHz louder than others of the same level.

The ear canal resonates near 3.4 kHz and boosts it by about 10 to 20 dB. The middle ear passes the sound from the air into the fluid of the cochlea, where a direct transition would transmit only about 0.1 percent of the energy.
The basilar membrane analyzes frequencies by place, high frequencies at the base and low ones at the apex. The Greenwood map grows with

children.html: log⁡(1+f/146 Hz)\log(1 + f / 146\,\text{Hz})log(1+f/146Hz)

children.value: , nearly linear at low and logarithmic at high frequencies, the same form as the mel scale with its knee at 700 Hz.

Outer hair cells amplify quiet sounds more than loud ones, inner hair cells transduce with a saturating response, and the nerve fibers adapt to constant sounds. Compression and adaptation are why audio features take logarithms of energies and why the onset strength counts only increases.

The primary auditory pathway runs from the cochlear nuclei through the superior olive, which compares the two ears, the inferior colliculus, and the thalamus to the tonotopic auditory cortex. Time differences of at most about 0.66 ms locate low frequencies, level differences caused by the head shadow locate high ones.

Several simultaneous pitches follow by iteration: estimate the strongest fundamental, subtract its harmonics, and repeat. Shared partials are the difficulty.

The autocorrelation of the onset strength has peaks at the beat period and its multiples. A log-Gaussian tempo prior around 0.5 s (120 bpm) with a width of 1.4 octaves selects the period a listener would most likely tap. The tempogram computes the autocorrelation in a sliding window and shows tempo changes.

Each phoneme has a left-to-right HMM with three emitting states. Emissions were first discrete symbols from a k-means codebook, then Gaussian mixtures; triphones with decision-tree state tying model the influence of the neighbors.

A pronunciation dictionary and an n-gram language model connect the phoneme models into one large HMM, which Viterbi decoding with a beam searches. Training needs only transcripts, no time alignment, but the dictionary limits the vocabulary.
A self-loop gives a geometric duration whose most likely value is one frame. Several states per phoneme, explicit duration models, and training data at varied rates handle the speaking rate.
Cepstral mean normalization removes the constant effect of a microphone or a line, and vocal tract length normalization warps the frequency axis per speaker. Neither addresses the speaking rate.

Hybrid HMM-DNN systems replaced the Gaussian mixtures with networks whose state posteriors, divided by the state priors, act as likelihoods. CTC removed the alignment, and encoder-decoder transformers such as Whisper replaced the whole chain.
Spoken content becomes searchable through its transcript or through phoneme n-grams; the latter finds words outside the vocabulary and tolerates partial recognition errors.
